strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: open-vocabulary object-goal navigation with lightweight, mapless policies and RGB input, which is relevant for embodied vision systems under sensor and compute constraints.

The empirical gains on HM3D-OVON are meaningful. With predicted YOLOE masks, OVSegDT reports 40.1 SR / 20.9 SPL on val unseen, improving over the main RGB-only DagRL baseline by a large margin and matching or exceeding several depth/odometry or large-model baselines on at least some metrics.

The ablation study is useful: the paper separates effects of EALM, goal-mask input, auxiliary segmentation loss, predicted-mask adaptation, and goal text versus mask. This makes clear that most of the final performance comes from the mask signal, while EALM improves training stability and collisions.

The paper reports multiple seeds for learned policies, collision counts as a safety-relevant metric, training curves, hyperparameters, compute details, and some statistical testing, which improves interpretability and reproducibility relative to many navigation papers.

The method is practically appealing in spirit: using an open-vocabulary segmenter to provide target masks to a compact transformer policy is simpler than full semantic mapping pipelines and could be useful when localization/depth are unreliable.
weaknesses: The central novelty is moderate. Adding a target-object mask to a navigation policy, using an auxiliary mask reconstruction loss, and adaptively mixing BC/PPO by entropy are plausible engineering choices, but the paper does not establish a deep technical advance beyond combining known ingredients effectively.

The strongest ground-truth-mask results are not representative of the deployable setting. Performance drops from about 70.4 SR / 39.4 SPL with GT masks to 40.1 SR / 20.9 SPL with calibrated YOLOE masks, showing that the method is highly dependent on external segmentation quality.

The detector calibration procedure raises fairness and generalization concerns. The paper tunes confidence thresholds per object category and analyzes category-specific success on validation splits; this may leak benchmark-specific knowledge and is not a realistic open-vocabulary protocol for arbitrary unseen categories. The final result depends substantially on this calibration.

The claim of being lightweight/RGB-only is somewhat misleading unless the YOLOE segmentation model and its inference cost are included. The policy may be 130M parameters, but the deployed system requires an additional open-vocabulary segmentation model whose compute, latency, and training data are not accounted for in the main comparison.

The auxiliary segmentation loss is weakly motivated technically. Since the model receives the target mask as input and reconstructs the current binary target mask, the task may mostly encourage copying/encoding the mask rather than learning semantic scene understanding from RGB. The ablation also shows it improves SR only slightly while reducing SPL and increasing collisions with GT masks.

The open-vocabulary/free-form language claim is overstated. The experiments appear to use category names from HM3D-OVON, and Table 11 shows that removing the mask causes almost complete failure, so the method relies far more on visual mask prompts than language understanding.

Comparisons to prior methods are not fully clean. Some baselines use different sensors or large models, while OVSegDT uses an external detector plus category-specific calibration; the paper should more carefully separate policy quality from detector quality and compare total system assumptions.

Reproducibility is only partial. The abstract says code is available but the link is blank in the extracted manuscript, and some important details of YOLOE threshold calibration, vocabulary pruning, and whether calibration uses validation labels are not specified enough to reproduce the headline deployable result confidently.

strengths: The paper tackles a relevant and difficult problem: open-vocabulary Object Goal Navigation under limited sensing, and it reports results on the established HM3D-OVON benchmark.

The target-mask conditioning idea is practically useful. With predicted YOLOE masks, the method reaches 40.1 SR / 20.9 SPL on val unseen, improving substantially over the cited DagRL baseline and remaining competitive with stronger sensor-based systems.

The ablations are reasonably broad: the paper separates training strategy, goal-mask input, auxiliary segmentation loss, and predicted-mask adaptation, and it reports multiple seeds for several key comparisons.
The method is computationally moderate compared with very large VLN/VLM systems, using a relatively small transformer policy and frozen SigLIP features.
weaknesses: The main performance gain appears to come from providing an external target segmentation mask, which largely delegates open-vocabulary recognition to YOLOE. This makes the contribution less clearly an end-to-end open-vocabulary navigation advance, and the paper underplays this dependency while claiming RGB-only, lightweight inference.

The predicted-mask result is much weaker than the ground-truth-mask result: val unseen drops from 70.4 SR / 39.4 SPL with GT masks to 40.1 SR / 20.9 SPL with calibrated YOLOE. This indicates that the central mechanism is highly sensitive to detector quality, a limitation acknowledged but not sufficiently analyzed for deployment.

The YOLOE calibration procedure raises fairness and reproducibility concerns. The manuscript describes category-specific confidence thresholds and vocabulary pruning, but does not clearly specify how these thresholds are selected without using validation categories or episodes, including unseen categories. This could leak benchmark-specific tuning into the reported val unseen numbers.

The claimed contribution of the auxiliary segmentation loss is weak. In Table 3 it improves SR only slightly under GT masks but worsens SPL and collisions, and there is no clear final-system ablation showing that it materially helps under predicted segmentation.

The evidence for EALM is not fully convincing. Its final val unseen gain over DagRL is modest in Table 2, the statistical appendix does not appear to establish significant EALM improvement on the most important unseen metrics, and the method is closer to an entropy-based loss scheduler than a clearly novel algorithmic contribution.

Several claims are overstated or imprecise. The paper claims state-of-the-art results, but Table 1 shows MTU3D has higher val unseen SR while OVSegDT has higher SPL; the method also relies on a large external segmentation model whose cost is not included in the 130M-parameter/lightweight framing.

The comparison to prior methods may not be fully controlled. Different methods use different sensors, modules, training budgets, and possibly external models, while the paper does not sufficiently normalize for detector/model cost or for the benefit of explicit object localization.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite hyperparameter tables. The abstract has an empty code link, the teacher/planner and DAgger data collection details are sparse, and the exact YOLOE fine-tuning/calibration recipe needed to reproduce the main result is underspecified.

The statistical analysis is fragile: only three seeds are used, one-sided unpaired t-tests are questionable for this setting, and several important comparisons are omitted. This weakens confidence in small reported gains.

The paper has notable presentation issues, including grammatical errors, inconsistent naming, and some ambiguous statements such as calling EALM per-sample while describing a mini-batch EMA gate. These are not the main reason for rejection, but they compound the clarity concerns.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem, open-vocabulary ObjectNav, with a practical emphasis on RGB-only mapless navigation. The proposed system is comparatively lightweight and avoids depth/odometry, which makes the setting attractive for deployment-constrained agents.

The empirical results on HM3D-OVON are strong. With predicted YOLOE masks, OVSegDT reaches 40.1 SR / 20.9 SPL on val unseen, substantially improving over the DagRL RGB-only baseline and competitive with or better than several methods that use additional sensors or larger vision-language modules.

The ablation study is useful and fairly broad: the paper separates the effects of EALM, goal-mask input, auxiliary segmentation loss, filtered-mask fine-tuning, and detector calibration. This makes clear that the main performance driver is target-mask conditioning, while EALM gives a smaller but meaningful improvement over the baseline training recipe.

The manuscript reports multiple metrics including SR, SPL, and collisions, includes training curves, three-seed reporting for several experiments, statistical tests, and hyperparameter/infrastructure details. This is stronger evidence than a single leaderboard-style comparison.

The idea of using segmentation masks as an explicit visual goal representation is simple but effective. The qualitative trajectories and the large gap between text-only and mask-conditioned inference support the claim that masks help the policy recognize when to switch from exploration to goal-directed navigation.
weaknesses: The final system depends heavily on the quality and calibration of an external open-vocabulary segmentation model. Performance drops from 70.4 SR with ground-truth masks to 35.5 SR with out-of-the-box YOLOE, and only reaches 40.1 after category-specific threshold/vocabulary calibration. This weakens the claim of robust open-vocabulary deployment and raises questions about how much validation/category information is used in calibration.

Some claims are overstated. The paper calls the method state of the art, but MTU3D has higher val-unseen SR in Table 1, albeit lower SPL and with extra sensors. The claim that EALM achieves the lowest collision count on val unseen is not supported by Table 2, where EarlySwitcher and DAgger+PPO have fewer collisions than EALM on that split.

The auxiliary segmentation loss has mixed evidence. In Table 3 it slightly increases SR but decreases SPL and increases collisions relative to goal-mask-only training. The justification for retaining it is mostly that SR is prioritized, but the tradeoff is material and should be framed more cautiously.

Originality is moderate rather than high. The architecture combines known components: frozen SigLIP encoders, a transformer policy, target masks from an external segmenter, auxiliary segmentation, and entropy-based objective mixing. The contribution is mainly an effective integration and empirical recipe rather than a fundamentally new navigation paradigm.

The evaluation is limited to HM3D-OVON simulation. There is no real-world validation, cross-dataset test, or analysis under different segmentation models beyond YOLOE. Since the method’s main limitation is segmentation quality, broader detector/domain robustness would be important evidence.

Reproducibility is not fully convincing. The abstract says code is available but the link appears blank, and the reproducibility checklist contains unfinished template entries. Details of the category-specific YOLOE calibration procedure are also insufficient to reproduce without potential validation-set tuning ambiguity.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely embodied vision problem: open-vocabulary object-goal navigation with limited sensing. The proposed OVSegDT combines RGB/text embeddings, a goal-mask encoder, transformer history, and a training recipe that is well matched to the task.

Empirical results on HM3D-OVON are strong. The reported val-unseen performance with predicted YOLOE masks reaches 44.7% SR and 20.6% SPL, improving substantially over the main RGB-only DagRL baseline and comparing favorably to several methods using depth/odometry or larger VLA/VLN systems.

The ablation study is useful and fairly detailed. The paper separately studies EALM, goal masks, semantic reward, auxiliary segmentation loss, detector calibration, predicted-mask fine-tuning, observation components, segmentation errors, and failure modes. This gives reasonable support to the main design choices.

The work is practically motivated: the method keeps a small navigation transformer, reports embedded inference latency, and includes real-robot demonstrations, which strengthens the potential usefulness beyond simulator-only benchmarks.

The paper is mostly clear and technically coherent. The architecture and losses are described sufficiently to understand the method, and the supplementary material includes important hyperparameters and statistical tests.
weaknesses: A central limitation is that much of the open-vocabulary generalization is delegated to the external segmentation model and its calibrated vocabulary. The text-only ablation collapses to near zero SR, indicating that OVSegDT itself has little open-vocabulary semantic ability without a high-quality mask. This weakens claims that the navigation policy itself generalizes semantically.

The evaluation depends on category-specific confidence threshold calibration and removal of semantically redundant categories. It is not fully clear whether this calibration uses validation categories/statistics in a way that would transfer to genuinely new user-specified categories. This is especially important because the method claims open-vocabulary behavior but also states that it lacks free-form instruction-following ability.

The training procedure uses privileged simulator information: geodesic distance, ground-truth target-mask area, and ground-truth masks during main training. This is acceptable for simulation training but should temper claims about sensor minimality and real-world transfer. The method uses only RGB at policy input, but the training signal and segmentation adaptation rely on privileged annotations.

The comparison to prior work is somewhat mixed. The method is described as lightweight and not using large vision-language models, but it relies on YOLOE for open-vocabulary segmentation and frozen SigLIP encoders. Comparisons against map-based or VLM/LLM systems with different sensing and compute assumptions are informative but not always apples-to-apples.

Safety remains a meaningful issue. Predicted-mask fine-tuning improves SR/SPL but roughly doubles collisions relative to the non-finetuned predicted-mask setting, and the real-robot section explicitly observes risky behavior near the goal. The paper prioritizes SR/SPL over collisions, but safe navigation is central to deployment.

Reproducibility has gaps. The abstract says code is available but the URL appears blank in the manuscript. Some implementation details are present, but reproducing the detector calibration, category vocabulary cleanup, and real-robot setup would require more precise protocol details.

There are several presentation and consistency issues: e.g., GPU memory is reported as thousands of Gb rather than likely MB, and some formatting/extraction artifacts make tables and equations harder to read. These are not fatal, but they should be corrected.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: open-vocabulary ObjectGoal navigation with reduced reliance on depth, odometry, explicit maps, or very large navigation models.

The proposed target-mask conditioning is simple and empirically effective. On HM3D-OVON val unseen, the reported final system improves over DagRL substantially in SR/SPL, and the ablations show that goal masks, EALM, semantic reward, and auxiliary segmentation loss each affect performance.

The manuscript includes useful diagnostic analyses beyond headline SR/SPL, including collision counts, failure categories, predicted-mask adaptation, segmentation error analysis, threshold sensitivity, and limited real-robot demonstrations.

The method is relatively lightweight compared with many VLM/LLM-based embodied navigation systems, and the reported Jetson Orin latency suggests practical promise if the segmentation dependency is acceptable.
weaknesses: A central claim of RGB-only, lightweight, mapless open-vocabulary navigation is weakened by the heavy dependence on an external open-vocabulary segmentation model and category-specific confidence calibration. The navigation policy fails almost completely with text alone, and performance drops sharply from GT masks to YOLOE masks, so much of the open-vocabulary capability is delegated to the detector/segmenter rather than learned by OVSegDT itself.

The evaluation protocol for segmentation calibration is insufficiently specified and potentially problematic. The paper discusses selecting category-dependent thresholds over the navigation vocabulary and provides analyses on validation splits, including unseen categories. If thresholds are tuned using val unseen navigation outcomes or target categories, the main generalization claim is overstated.

The final predicted-mask fine-tuned model improves SR/SPL but greatly increases collisions compared with the non-finetuned predicted-mask variants. The paper downplays this by prioritizing SR/SPL, yet safety is a major embodied navigation concern and the real-robot section explicitly reports risky behavior near goals.

Several training signals rely on simulator privileged information, especially geodesic distance and ground-truth target-mask area in the semantic reward, including during adaptation to predicted masks. This is acceptable for simulator training, but it limits the strength of claims about real-world deployability and sim-to-real transfer.

The experimental breadth is narrow: the main evidence is on HM3D-OVON, with only demonstration-level real-world results and no rigorous comparison under alternative segmenters, different detectors, unseen synonym/phrase settings beyond the benchmark, or transfer to other simulators/datasets.

The comparison to prior work is not fully clean. The table emphasizes no depth/odometry and no large VLM, but the method uses a strong pretrained open-vocabulary segmenter; this external perception module is not accounted for as carefully as the modules used by map-based or VLM-based baselines.
The statistical analysis is weak: three seeds with one-sided t-tests and multiple comparisons is not very convincing, and some conclusions are stronger than the evidence supports.

Reproducibility has gaps. The abstract says code is available but no URL is present, detector calibration details are not fully operationalized, and important implementation choices around YOLOE vocabulary pruning/threshold selection would be hard to reproduce exactly.

There are presentation and consistency issues that reduce confidence: e.g., implausible GPU memory units in the supplement, overclaiming of state-of-the-art despite mixed comparisons, and occasional unclear descriptions of whether masks/rewards are predicted or ground truth in each training stage.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and current problem: open-vocabulary object-goal navigation with a lightweight, mapless policy using RGB input. The framing is useful because it explores a middle ground between heavy map/LLM-based systems and weaker end-to-end baselines.

The empirical results on HM3D-OVON are strong, especially on the val unseen split: OVSegDT reports 44.7% SR and 20.6% SPL with predicted YOLOE masks, outperforming the cited RGB-only and several depth/odometry baselines in success rate.

The ablations are meaningful. The paper separately studies EALM, goal-mask input, semantic reward, auxiliary segmentation loss, predicted-mask fine-tuning, confidence calibration, and observation components, making the source of gains more interpretable than in many navigation papers.

The adaptation-to-predicted-segmentation analysis is valuable. The large gap between GT masks and YOLOE masks is made explicit, and the authors analyze failure modes, false positives/false negatives, threshold sensitivity, latency, and some real-robot demonstrations.

The method is practically attractive in its core form: a 130M-parameter transformer with frozen SigLIP features and a lightweight mask encoder is simpler and potentially more deployable than approaches requiring large VLM/LLM planners or explicit semantic maps.
weaknesses: The strongest claim, open-vocabulary generalization, is somewhat weakened by dependence on an external open-vocabulary segmentation model plus category-specific confidence calibration and vocabulary pruning. If thresholds are tuned using the benchmark navigation vocabulary or validation categories, including unseen categories, this may partly compromise the open-vocabulary evaluation protocol.

The comparison to prior work is not fully apples-to-apples. OVSegDT does not use depth or odometry, but it does receive a powerful segmentation-derived visual cue from YOLOE; this is a different kind of external perceptual support from methods that use only RGB/text embeddings. The paper should be more careful in how it phrases superiority over methods without such masks.

Safety remains a serious limitation. The final predicted-mask model improves SR/SPL but increases collisions substantially compared with the non-finetuned YOLOE variants, and the real-robot section explicitly reports risky near-goal behavior. This matters for an embodied navigation paper, even if SR/SPL are strong.

The novelty of EALM is useful but incremental: entropy-based scheduling between imitation and RL is a reasonable heuristic rather than a deeply new algorithmic idea, and the derivation of entropy thresholds is only lightly justified. The paper would be stronger with broader comparisons to tuned schedules or other adaptive IL/RL mixing strategies under the same architecture.

The method is not truly free-form instruction following despite some language in the paper; it mainly handles object category names, and the authors acknowledge lack of free-form text instruction ability. This should be stated more prominently to avoid overstating the scope.

Reproducibility is only moderate from the manuscript. Hyperparameters and ablations are included, but the code link appears blank in the provided PDF, and important details of segmentation-threshold calibration, vocabulary pruning, and whether calibration uses validation/unseen categories need to be specified precisely.
